questions.text: What do PostgreSQL object privileges determine?

answers.text: Which actions a role may perform on a specific object
Only how the role password is stored
The physical path to table files

questions.explanation: The lecture describes privileges as the relationship between a subject — a role — and an object, defining the actions available to that role.

questions.text: Which of the listed privileges apply to PostgreSQL tables? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE are table object privileges. LOGIN is a role attribute.

questions.text: Which privilege allows reading data from a table or view?
questions.explanation: The slide directly maps SELECT to reading data.

questions.text: Which mappings between table privileges and actions are correct? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: The notes list DELETE, TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, and REFERENCES among table privileges.

questions.text: Which command grants a privilege to a role?
questions.explanation: GRANT is used to provide object privileges and role membership.

questions.text: What can GRANT and REVOKE do? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Change the physical storage format of a table

questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL, GRANT and REVOKE apply both to object privileges and to role membership.

questions.text: Which role category model bypasses normal access-control checks?

answers.text: All members of the public role

questions.explanation: The lecture treats superusers as a separate category: normal access-control checks are not performed for them.

questions.text: Which statements about an object owner are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The owner initially receives all privileges for its object
The owner can grant and revoke privileges on its object
Some owner actions are not represented by ordinary object privileges
The owner always automatically becomes a superuser

questions.explanation: The material emphasizes the owner's special position, including the ability to drop the object and manage its privileges.

questions.text: What determines access for an ordinary role that is neither a superuser nor the object owner?

answers.text: Only the presence of the LOGIN attribute
Only the order of rows in pg_hba.conf
The physical location of the object

questions.explanation: The third category in the lecture is other roles, whose access to an object is limited by granted privileges.

questions.text: Which statements about group roles are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They are used to group privilege sets
Such roles are usually created with NOLOGIN
An ordinary role can be made a member of a group role
A group role must have SUPERUSER

questions.explanation: The notes define a group role as a convenient named set of privileges that can be assigned to users through membership.

questions.text: What is the PUBLIC pseudo-role?

answers.text: An implicit group that includes all roles
The name of the mandatory superuser
A role only for database owners
A system role for running autovacuum

questions.explanation: If a privilege is granted to PUBLIC, it effectively becomes available to all roles because PUBLIC implicitly includes them.

questions.text: Which statements about role membership and attributes are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Roles can be made members of other roles
Such membership is useful for privilege management
Attributes of a containing role are not inherited in the same way as object privileges
Membership automatically makes every role a superuser

questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly notes that role attributes are not inherited like ordinary privileges; when necessary, a session can switch to the containing role.

questions.text: How do you list roles in psql, including predefined system roles?
questions.explanation: The notes show \duS for displaying the complete role list, including predefined roles.

questions.text: What can the default-privileges mechanism do? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Automatically grant privileges when new objects are created
Automatically revoke specified privileges for new objects
Configure future privileges for objects created by a particular role
Retroactively change privileges on all existing objects automatically

questions.explanation: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES affects privileges on objects that will be created in the future; it is not a bulk replacement of privileges on existing objects.

questions.text: Which object privilege applies to PostgreSQL functions and procedures?
questions.explanation: For functions and procedures, the material identifies a single object privilege: EXECUTE.

questions.text: Which statements about SECURITY INVOKER and SECURITY DEFINER are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: SECURITY INVOKER runs the routine with the privileges of the calling role
SECURITY DEFINER runs the routine with the privileges of its owner
SECURITY INVOKER is the default in the shown material
SECURITY DEFINER automatically turns the calling role into a superuser

questions.explanation: The distinction is the privilege context in which the code runs: the calling user or the routine owner.

questions.text: Which mappings between PostgreSQL object types and privileges are correct? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: The privilege set depends on object type: a tablespace has CREATE; a database has CONNECT/CREATE/TEMPORARY; a schema has USAGE/CREATE; and a sequence has SELECT/UPDATE/USAGE.

questions.text: Which privileges does PostgreSQL 16 grant to PUBLIC by default for newly created objects of the corresponding types? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: USAGE for languages and data types
SELECT for all newly created user tables

questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL 16, PUBLIC automatically receives some privileges: CONNECT/TEMPORARY on databases, EXECUTE on functions and procedures, and USAGE on languages and types. PUBLIC does not receive SELECT on user tables by default.

questions.text: What are PostgreSQL has_*_privilege functions intended for?

answers.text: Check whether a role has a specified privilege on an object
Change the authentication method in pg_hba.conf

questions.explanation: After discussing role categories, the material points to the has_*_privilege family as a way to programmatically test for a specific privilege on an object.

questions.text: Which measures belong to safe use of a SECURITY DEFINER function? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Remove schemas writable by untrusted users from search_path
Place pg_temp at the end of a safe search_path
Restrict EXECUTE if the function should not be available to everyone through PUBLIC
Always grant SUPERUSER to calling roles

questions.explanation: SECURITY DEFINER runs with the owner's privileges, so the linked documentation requires a protected search_path; for sensitive functions, the automatically granted PUBLIC EXECUTE privilege should also be controlled.

questions.text: Which mappings between predefined PostgreSQL roles and their purposes are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: pg_read_all_data — read data from all tables, views, and sequences with the necessary schema USAGE privileges
pg_write_all_data — write data without automatically getting BYPASSRLS

questions.explanation: Predefined roles allow administrative capabilities to be delegated without SUPERUSER. pg_monitor and related monitoring roles provide limited access to system information, while pg_read_all_data/pg_write_all_data provide data access without automatically bypassing RLS.
